edition.deck: A deadly shooting outside Paris, new escalation threats in the West Bank and uncertainty over Ukraine’s satellite links lead the day’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises significant developments and fresh reporting. Allegations, preliminary findings and unconfirmed claims are clearly attributed; longer-running stories are included only where today’s material adds a meaningful development.

content.headline: Paris-area shootings kill one as terrorism inquiry examines racist motive
content.shortHeadline: Paris-area shootings kill one as terrorism inquiry examines motive
content.standfirst: A suspected gunman was arrested after a series of shootings near Paris left one person dead and five wounded. Authorities are investigating a possible terrorist offence; the motive has not been established.

image.caption: Emergency services at the scene of the shooting near Paris.

sources.originalTitle: Deadly shooting near Paris investigated as 'crime of terrorism', minister says
Efter skyderi i Paris: Indenrigsminister kalder det terror

segments.body: One person was killed and five others wounded, three seriously, in shootings in Trappes and nearby La Verrière on Friday, French authorities said. A suspected attacker was arrested. The anti-terror prosecutor is investigating whether the killings were connected to a terrorist enterprise.

perspectives.body: Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh described the attack as having racist, possibly Islamophobic, undertones. The prosecutor has urged caution about the victims’ identities, and the motive remains unclear.

segments.body: The shootings lasted about 15 minutes, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. The prosecutor’s investigation also includes whether offences were committed because of a victim’s real or perceived race, ethnicity, nationality or religion; no motive has been confirmed.

content.headline: White House says Ukraine-Russia truce agreed for besieged Oleshky
content.shortHeadline: White House announces proposed truce for Ukraine’s Oleshky
content.standfirst: The White House says a local ceasefire will begin on 29 October to allow aid deliveries and evacuations from the Russian-occupied city. Kyiv and Moscow have not confirmed the agreement.

image.caption: Residents who were able to leave Oleshky in the spring.

sources.originalTitle: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis

segments.body: The White House says Russia and Ukraine have agreed to halt military operations in Oleshky from 29 October, allowing humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations to evacuate civilians. Neither government has publicly confirmed the arrangement. The statement does not say how long the ceasefire would last.

segments.title: A city in crisis
segments.body: Residents face severe shortages of food, water and electricity; some have reportedly survived on weeds and boiled grass. Ukraine has been seeking an evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, and has used drones to drop emergency supplies, the Guardian reports.

content.headline: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions persist as it explores satellite alternative
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine reports Starlink problems and explores its own satellite links
content.standfirst: Ukraine says it has not confirmed that restrictions on its military satellite service have been lifted, despite Donald Trump’s claim. Kyiv has signed a preliminary agreement to explore a system it could control itself.

image.caption: A Ukrainian soldier installs a Starlink communications system on an attack drone.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted
Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row?
Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis
Ukrainerne vil bygge deres eget satellit-netværk og gøre sig frie af Elon Musk

segments.body: Ukrainian defence ministry sources told the BBC that connectivity problems continue, including drones losing connection at speeds above about 161km/h. A Ukrainian military expert told the Guardian that isolated cases above the limit did not show that restrictions had been lifted. Trump has said Elon Musk restored the service.

segments.title: Seeking a backup
segments.body: Ukraine has signed a statement of intent with Finnish companies Nokia and Iceye to explore a satellite network it could control. It is not a final contract. Defence analyst Jakob Clod Asmund told DR that replacing Starshield would be difficult, but a separate system could provide a backup if access to the current one were cut.

perspectives.body: Asmund compared the proposed network to an emergency generator: not necessarily a direct replacement for Starshield, but a way to reduce reliance on a service that others can switch off.

content.headline: Netanyahu threatens major West Bank operation after two Israeli soldiers killed
content.shortHeadline: Netanyahu threatens major West Bank operation after deadly Hebron gunﬁ
content.standfirst: Two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian attackers were killed in a gun battle near Hebron, according to Israeli reporting. Benjamin Netanyahu has threatened house searches and demolitions as tensions rise ahead of Israel’s election.

image.caption: Israeli forces patrol Hebron as Benjamin Netanyahu visits the area.

sources.originalTitle: Two Israeli soldiers killed in attack by suspected Palestinian gunmen in West Bank
Netanyahu orders ‘very extensive’ operation in West Bank after two Israeli soldiers killed
Netanyahu varsler militæraktion på Vestbredden

segments.body: Two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian attackers were killed in a gun battle near a checkpoint outside Hebron, according to the Israeli military and reporting by the Guardian and DR. Three other Israelis were wounded. The military said the attackers had opened fire and that it believed they intended to reach a nearby highway.

segments.title: Threat of wider action
segments.body: Netanyahu has ordered preparations for what he called a very extensive operation, including entering the attackers’ neighbourhood, evacuating residents and demolishing homes. He has not given a date. The statements come days before Israel’s election, amid rising settler violence and restrictions in the occupied West Bank.

perspectives.body: Human rights advocates warned that the attack could be used to justify tougher measures against Palestinians. The Guardian also reported concerns about displacement and the prospect of further curfews and demolitions.

content.headline: Six killed and 28 injured in shooting at church funeral in Jordan
content.shortHeadline: Six killed in shooting at church funeral in Jordan
content.standfirst: Gunmen opened fire during a funeral in the southern Karak governorate, Jordanian officials say. No one has claimed responsibility and a manhunt is under way.

image.caption: The church in Karak where gunmen opened fire during a funeral.

sources.originalTitle: Six shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say
Seks personer har mistet livet, og 28 er såret efter et skyderi ved en kirke i Jordan

segments.body: Six people were killed and 28 injured when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in the village of Hmoud, in Jordan’s Karak governorate, officials said. The attackers fled, and authorities have launched a manhunt. No one has claimed responsibility.

A witness told state television that two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol fired for several minutes. The BBC verified footage that appears to show three armed men approaching the church. Authorities have not confirmed a motive or identified those responsible.

content.headline: Personalised melanoma vaccine cuts recurrence or death risk by 42% in trial
content.shortHeadline: Personalised melanoma vaccine cuts recurrence or death risk by 42%
content.standfirst: In a trial of 1,137 adults, an experimental personalised mRNA vaccine given with Keytruda reduced the reported risk of melanoma returning or death. Longer follow-up is needed, and results have not yet appeared in a peer-reviewed journal.

image.caption: Tony Chapman, who took part in the melanoma vaccine trial.

sources.originalTitle: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial

segments.body: The trial found that patients given the personalised vaccine Intismeran alongside Keytruda had a 42% lower risk of melanoma returning or death than patients given Keytruda alone. The companies say the approach is also being tested against other cancers, but the vaccine is not approved.

segments.title: Evidence still developing
segments.body: Independent experts called the findings promising but cautioned that longer follow-up is needed to assess whether the treatment improves overall survival. The full results are due to be presented at a conference in Madrid on Saturday and have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed medical journal.

content.headline: US judge halts voter-fraud probes as midterm election dispute grows
content.shortHeadline: US judge questions voter-fraud probes ahead of midterms
content.standfirst: A federal judge says the Justice Department relied on flawed data in investigations of possible non-citizen voting. The ruling was put on hold until Friday to allow an appeal, leaving its immediate effect uncertain.

image.caption: People cast early votes in Nashville, Tennessee.

sources.originalTitle: Why US court order could have just given Trump excuse to enact ‘doomsday’ plans

segments.body: A federal judge ordered the Justice Department to halt investigations into non-citizen voting in nine states, finding that its data could wrongly identify eligible voters and that the probes risked intimidating groups helping voters. The ruling was stayed until Friday to give the department time to appeal.

Non-citizen voting is already illegal and rare, the report says. Attorney General Todd Blanche declined to rule out legal action challenging the certification of midterm results in a hypothetical case involving widespread fraud. The department has also appealed a separate dispute with California over voter rolls.

content.headline: Texas Hispanic voters signal possible shift away from Trump, polls suggest
content.shortHeadline: Texas Hispanic voters may be turning against Trump, polls suggest
content.standfirst: Interviews and recent polling in the Rio Grande Valley suggest some Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024 are uneasy with his immigration crackdown. Polls are uncertain, and the election is still to come.

image.caption: Father Roy Snipes, known locally as the Cowboy Priest, opposed plans for a border wall near his chapel.

sources.originalTitle: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning

segments.body: Recent surveys suggest a majority of Hispanic voters in Texas disapprove of Trump and favour Democrats ahead of the 3 November midterms. The BBC’s reporting in the Rio Grande Valley finds voters who supported tougher border controls but oppose the treatment of migrants and the reach of immigration enforcement.

The account describes a close congressional contest in Texas’s 15th district, which was redrawn to give Republicans a notional advantage but where polling suggests a Democratic lead. Polls are not a guarantee of the result, and turnout may prove decisive.

content.headline: Government to intervene in next water-bill review and investment plans
content.shortHeadline: Ministers to intervene in next water-bill review and investment plans
content.standfirst: Environment secretary Angela Eagle has told water companies and regulators to prioritise affordable bills, leak prevention and sewage reduction. Campaigners say the measures do not promise lower bills or settle the question of public ownership.

image.caption: Water companies have been told to prioritise preventing leaks and sewage spills.

sources.originalTitle: UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills
Burnham’s plan to fix sewage crisis and lower water bills ‘could fail’. This is why

segments.body: The government plans to intervene in the next five-year water price review, which is run by Ofwat and is expected to conclude in 2029. Eagle’s letter asks companies and regulators to focus on value for money, affordable bills, technology, leaks and sewage. It stops short of demanding bill cuts.

segments.title: Pressure for deeper reform
segments.body: The Guardian reports that ministers intend to use the price review to influence investment before wider changes are set out. Separately, 28 Labour MPs have called for an independent study of public-ownership models, saying current proposals fall short. The government says nothing is off the table.

perspectives.body: The MPs are asking for a feasibility study comparing national, local and mutual ownership, including their effects on bills and the environment. Their call highlights that the government has not yet committed to taking water companies into public ownership.

content.headline: Storm Austen leaves thousands without power as second storm approaches
content.shortHeadline: Thousands lose power as Storm Austen hits south-west England
content.standfirst: More than 16,000 homes in south-west England were without power on Friday morning and some Cornwall schools were disrupted. A further amber wind warning is forecast as Storm Boelo approaches parts of the UK.

image.caption: A tree brought down by Storm Austen blocks a pavement in Falmouth, Cornwall.

sources.originalTitle: Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England

segments.body: Storm Austen brought winds of up to 76mph to the Isles of Scilly and left more than 16,000 homes in the south-west without power shortly before 11am, according to National Grid. Schools in Cornwall were disrupted and rail services faced cancellations. The grid said power had been restored to more than 12,000 properties by 8am.

segments.title: More severe weather forecast
segments.body: The Met Office has issued an amber wind warning for Storm Boelo from Saturday evening into Sunday, covering parts of Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England. It warns of possible power cuts, damage and transport disruption, with gusts of up to 80mph in exposed coastal areas.

content.headline: Britain faces high energy costs as winter supply relies on imports
content.shortHeadline: Britain faces high energy costs as winter imports rise
content.standfirst: Britain is forecast to have enough gas and electricity this winter, but operators expect it to pay high prices to secure imports. Brent crude also rose above $115 a barrel amid fears of renewed strikes on Iran.

image.caption: A snowy London street as Britain prepares for winter energy demand.

sources.originalTitle: Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter
Oil price rises above $115 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran

segments.body: Great Britain is expected to rely more on imported gas and electricity this winter, with system operators saying supply should meet demand at a higher cost. Gas storage is low across Europe, and UK buyers may have to compete for liquefied natural gas cargoes. Ofgem approved a pipeline deal that adds about 10p a month to the average gas bill.

segments.title: Conflict adds pressure to oil markets
segments.body: Brent crude rose above $115 a barrel on Friday, its highest level since May, after Iran threatened attacks on Gulf infrastructure if a new US-Israeli offensive is launched. Analysts cited fears of renewed strikes, danger to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on Saudi facilities as supply concerns.

content.headline: Free Speech Union faces staff allegations of racism and inappropriate remarks
content.shortHeadline: Free Speech Union faces staff allegations of racism and misconduct
content.standfirst: The Guardian reports that former and current staff made complaints about senior figures at the campaign group. The people accused declined to comment; founder Toby Young said he could not discuss internal employment matters.

image.caption: The Free Speech Union was founded by Toby Young.

sources.originalTitle: Free Speech Union hit by internal allegations of racism and sexually inappropriate remarks

segments.body: Staff at the Free Speech Union alleged that its former chief operating officer, Sigrun Olafsdottir, said she would “never hire a black person”. Staff also described remarks about actor Sydney Sweeney’s body by legislative affairs director Sam Armstrong. The Guardian says it has spoken to multiple sources and reviewed documentation related to parts of the claims.

segments.title: The organisation’s response
segments.body: Olafsdottir and Armstrong declined to comment. Founder Toby Young said he could not comment on internal employment matters; he said a discussion involving Sweeney related to a member’s case and was not untoward or unprofessional. The report also says eight staff members have left in the past year.

content.headline: Meghan says she was told of allegations against father in 2018
content.shortHeadline: Meghan says police told her of allegations against father in 2018
content.standfirst: The Duchess of Sussex says she was informed of “disturbing allegations” about her estranged father and trusted authorities to investigate. Thomas Markle denies possessing child sexual abuse images; Philippine authorities are examining a computer.

image.caption: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex.

sources.originalTitle: Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018
Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father

segments.body: Meghan said a letter containing allegations about Thomas Markle was sent to the Metropolitan Police in 2018 and later shared with her. She said she was assured the allegations were being investigated and that her decision to keep her children from her father was intended to protect them.

segments.title: Investigations and denial
segments.body: Philippine officials told the BBC that a taskforce is investigating and that national police have secured Markle’s computer for digital examination. The BBC says the Metropolitan Police is not currently investigating him, but is making internal inquiries about the handling of the 2018 letter. Markle denies possessing the images.

content.headline: UK and EU talks face pressure over Ukraine aid and youth mobility
content.shortHeadline: UK and EU face pressure over Ukraine aid and reset-summit talks
content.standfirst: EU leaders are expected to urge Britain to contribute more towards Ukraine’s 2027 funding gap at a November summit. Separately, youth mobility and tuition fees remain unsettled parts of the UK-EU reset talks.

image.caption: Andy Burnham is due to attend a UK-EU reset summit in Brussels on 20 November.

sources.originalTitle: EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence
Youth mobility scheme may be delayed to ensure success of UK-EU summit
Major obstacle removed for UK to clinch Brexit deal within weeks

segments.body: Ukraine says it faces a €70bn shortfall in 2027 for defence and civilian needs. EU officials say member states cover most of its financial needs and will ask the UK to increase support when Andy Burnham meets EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November. The UK says it has committed £25bn to Ukraine.

segments.title: Other summit issues remain open
segments.body: The summit agenda also includes food and animal-health arrangements, links between emissions trading systems and a youth mobility scheme. Reports differ on whether the EU can defer the tuition-fee dispute: the i Paper says France and Germany have signalled they may be willing to do so, while the Guardian reports no consensus among member states. Visa numbers also remain unresolved.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports that France and Germany have signalled willingness to postpone the tuition-fee question to avoid jeopardising the summit, but says the compromise is not settled and EU governments have not reached consensus.

content.headline: New forensic analysis challenges part of Jeremy Bamber murder case
content.shortHeadline: Forensic analysis challenges prosecution account in Bamber case
content.standfirst: A Guardian-commissioned expert says blood patterns in the 1985 White House Farm killings are consistent with Sheila Caffell shooting herself, but cannot establish who killed the other four victims. Essex police say Jeremy Bamber remains responsible.

sources.originalTitle: The White House Farm massacre - exclusive: new forensic evidence suggests Sheila Caffell killed herself. Is Jeremy Bamber innocent?

segments.title: What the new analysis says
segments.body: Forensic biologist Sue Carney-Gannon analysed crime-scene photographs and concluded that blood patterns on Caffell’s clothing are consistent with her being seated when shot and falling backwards. She says the patterns support the possibility of suicide, but cannot determine whether Caffell killed the rest of her family or whether Bamber did.

segments.title: A disputed conviction
segments.body: The analysis challenges the prosecution account that Bamber staged Caffell’s suicide after killing her. The Guardian also reports that the crime scene was heavily contaminated and that a previous expert called by the prosecution could not rule out suicide. Essex police say several appeals and reviews have upheld Bamber’s responsibility for the five murders.

segments.title: What happens next
segments.body: The new findings are to be given to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, which has so far considered four of ten points in Bamber’s latest submission and rejected those four. The analysis is evidence for the commission to assess, not a court finding that the conviction is unsafe.

content.headline: Danish teenager’s mother says espionage case is a “terrible misunderstanding”
content.shortHeadline: Mother of Danish espionage suspect calls case a misunderstanding
content.standfirst: An 18-year-old is accused of photographing a defence company for Russian intelligence, according to the charge. His mother says he believed he was collecting a free television; the evidence has not been made public because the hearing was closed.

sources.originalTitle: Mor til 18-årig spionagesigtet: 'Det er en frygtelig misforståelse'

segments.body: A Ukrainian mother told DR she believes her 18-year-old son was caught in a “terrible misunderstanding”. He and a 21-year-old man are charged with spying for Russian intelligence after allegedly photographing defence company MyDefence in Aalborg and sending the images via Telegram.

segments.title: Evidence not public
segments.body: The mother says her son answered an online post offering a free television and microwave and did not know he was being recruited for espionage. The men were held for three days while police gathered evidence; because the preliminary hearing was closed, the public has not seen the evidence in the case.

content.headline: Government criticised for unclear criteria for pension top-up
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s pension top-up criteria remain unclear
content.standfirst: The government plans an extra 1,000 kroner a month after tax for 150,000 pensioners, but has not said how recipients will be chosen. Its refusal to confirm whether a pensioner pictured with Mette Frederiksen qualifies has drawn criticism.

image.caption: Mette Frederiksen shared a post showing her shopping with pensioner Annemarie.

sources.originalTitle: Annemarie var på indkøbstur med statsministeren: Men S garanterer ikke, at hun er en af de pensionister, der får 1.000 kroner

segments.body: The government has said 150,000 of Denmark’s 1.1 million pensioners will receive an extra 1,000 kroner a month after tax. It has not disclosed the criteria for deciding who qualifies, leaving pensioners unable to know whether they will receive the payment.

Socialdemokratiet did not say whether Annemarie, pictured shopping with Mette Frederiksen, would receive the top-up. The Danish People’s Party and Ældre Sagen criticised the lack of clarity and argued that more low-income pensioners should be helped.

content.headline: MP Jacob Harris barred from company leadership for three years
content.shortHeadline: Danish MP Jacob Harris barred from company leadership for three years
content.standfirst: A Danish bankruptcy court imposed a three-year disqualification on independent MP Jacob Harris and his wife over the collapse of their construction company. The court cited poor or missing accounts and payments it considered largely private.

image.caption: Jacob Harris, now an independent member of Denmark’s parliament.

sources.originalTitle: Løsgængeren Jacob Harris er idømt konkurskarantæne

segments.body: A court in Roskilde has barred MP Jacob Harris and his wife from leading or serving on the board of a company for three years. The ruling relates to their construction firm Krokodille ApS, which went bankrupt last year.

segments.title: Court findings and next steps
segments.body: The court cited deficient bookkeeping, including no accounts for 2025, and substantial payments that appeared from their descriptions to be personal rather than connected with the company. Harris has said earlier that expenses were related to business activity and that any mistakes were not intentional. His lawyer has not said whether the couple will appeal; a separate compensation case is pending.

content.headline: First bird-flu outbreak of the season prompts cull of 40,000 turkeys
content.shortHeadline: 40,000 turkeys to be culled after bird flu found in Slagelse
content.standfirst: Authorities confirmed highly pathogenic avian influenza at a turkey farm in Bøgelunde, Slagelse Municipality. The birds are to be culled and protection and surveillance zones have been established.

sources.originalTitle: 40.000 kalkuner aflives efter fund af fugleinfluenza i Slagelse Kommune

segments.body: Laboratory results confirmed Denmark’s first reported outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza in a poultry flock this season, the Danish Veterinary and Food Administration said. The affected farm in Bøgelunde holds 40,000 turkeys, which are to be culled on Saturday.

Authorities have established protection and surveillance zones around the farm. Poultry owners inside them must register their birds and may not move live birds, eggs or poultry products without special permission. The agency urged owners to keep wild birds away from domestic birds, feed and water.

content.headline: North Jutland leaders meet over long waits for children’s assessments
content.shortHeadline: North Jutland leaders seek action on children’s long assessment waits
content.standfirst: Families in North Jutland are waiting more than a year for some children to be assessed for autism or ADHD. Regional and municipal leaders met to discuss how to improve support and reduce delays.

sources.originalTitle: 'Det er lidt en katastrofe': Nordjyske børn venter halvandet år på udredning - og det skal laves om

segments.body: Eva Catharina Bandholm’s family waited more than a year for her daughter to receive a diagnosis, she told DR. She said the delay meant they knew their child needed help but could not get support started at school.

More than 100 politicians and local and regional officials attended a meeting in Vrå to discuss growing numbers of children and young people in distress. North Jutland leaders said they would work towards more ambitious goals after the meeting, but the report gives no specific timeline or agreed measures.

content.headline: Danish national receives further sentence in €200m VAT fraud case
content.shortHeadline: Dane receives further prison term in €200m VAT fraud case
content.standfirst: A court in Düsseldorf sentenced a Danish national to five years and eight months for additional offences linked to a cross-border electronics fraud network. He had already received a separate sentence in the case.

image.caption: Items seized during the Goliath investigation included luxury cars and a high-value watch.

sources.originalTitle: Dansker idømt endnu en lang straf i svindelsag på 1,5 milliarder kroner

segments.body: A Danish national has received a five-year-and-eight-month prison sentence in Germany for supporting a criminal organisation and involvement in five cases of VAT fraud, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office said. The ruling concerns separate offences in the wider case.

segments.title: A cross-border scheme
segments.body: The network is accused of defrauding EU countries of €200m, about 1.5bn kroner, between 2019 and 2023 through sham electronics trades, mainly involving AirPods. The Dane was previously sentenced to five years and two months in the same investigation. The latest sentence adds to that earlier ruling.

content.headline: Security checks cause long queues at Copenhagen Airport
content.shortHeadline: Extra security checks cause long queues at Copenhagen Airport
content.standfirst: At least 250 SAS passengers had missed their flights by Thursday as temporary additional security checks caused queues of up to an hour. Authorities have not disclosed what prompted the extra measures.

image.caption: Passengers queue at Copenhagen Airport during the security delays.

sources.originalTitle: Kaotiske tilstande i Københavns Lufthavn efter øget krav til sikkerhed

segments.body: Passengers faced long queues at Copenhagen Airport after the Danish Transport Authority required temporary additional security measures. SAS said 250 passengers had missed flights by Thursday and that it was working to rebook them. The airport said waits could reach an hour.

The airport said the measures would remain in place at least through the weekend and advised passengers to arrive two hours before Schengen flights and three hours before flights outside Schengen. Neither the authority nor the airport disclosed what had prompted the extra requirements.

content.headline: Are phones, drugs and chatter changing what the dancefloor is for?
content.shortHeadline: The fight over talking on the dancefloor
content.standfirst: A DJ’s plea for less chatter has opened up a bigger debate about club etiquette, phones, drugs and who gets to shape a night out. DJs and dancers disagree on whether conversation disrupts community or helps make it.

sources.originalTitle: Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?

segments.body: DJ Jane Fitz’s request for people to talk less during sets struck a nerve: some clubbers welcomed it, while others argued that paying to get in means they should be free to chat. The debate also reflects changes in club life, from phone filming and rising costs to packed venues with few places to step away from the music.

segments.title: A shared space, different expectations
segments.body: For some DJs, ketamine and phone use leave dancers isolated or watching rather than moving; others see conversation as part of the connection that makes clubbing matter. Venues are trying practical fixes, from phone-camera stickers and no-phone rules to spaces that direct dancers and talkers in different directions.

perspectives.body: The reporting finds no simple consensus: DJ Dan Beaumont argues that clubbing needs an equilibrium of “yappers and dancers”, while Jane Fitz says she has already noticed dancefloors becoming quieter during breakdowns.

content.headline: Raye’s Mercury win makes a case for the ambitious album
content.shortHeadline: Raye wins the Mercury with an album-sized statement
content.standfirst: This Music May Contain Hope takes the 2026 prize after a career that moved from label conflict to major success. The win also raises questions about whether the Mercury still champions records beyond the commercial mainstream.

image.caption: Raye accepts the 2026 Mercury prize.

sources.originalTitle: Raye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain Hope
With albums under threat, Raye’s Mercury win is a triumph for grand statements

segments.body: Raye won the 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain Hope, a 73-minute, 17-track album that moves across styles and is structured in four sections. The singer said she was grateful to be recognised for an album after earlier years in which, she said, the focus was on singles.

segments.title: What the award celebrates
segments.body: The Guardian’s review welcomes the record’s scale and risk-taking, while noting that its length also makes room for self-indulgent passages. It argues that the prize needs to support such expansive statements—but asks whether it will also reward ambitious work by less-established artists.

perspectives.body: The review sees the win as a defence of the album form, but cautions that recent victories for commercially successful records leave an open question: will the Mercury also make space for underground artists?

content.headline: A Taylor Swift fan remembers the Myspace days before fame
content.shortHeadline: Before Taylor Swift was famous, Myspace made fans feel close
content.standfirst: Twenty years after Swift’s debut, a former teenage fan recalls discovering her online and feeling part of her rise. The personal history charts how direct connection with fans helped turn a young country singer into a global star.

image.caption: Taylor Swift emerged as a teenage country singer before her rise to global fame.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on Myspace in 2006

segments.body: The writer first found Taylor Swift through a friend’s Myspace page, before Swift released her self-titled debut in 2006. As teenagers, she and her friends followed the singer’s posts, collected press clippings and traded songs, finding in that early online fandom a shared identity as well as music.

segments.title: A relationship built online
segments.body: Swift’s direct updates and messages made her seem like a familiar peer to young fans, even as a savvy team helped shape her public image. The writer looks back on the distance between that sense of intimacy and the enormous fame Swift later achieved—and on how her ambition expanded what young women could imagine for themselves.

content.headline: Beirut City Pop revisits the music made amid Lebanon’s civil war
content.shortHeadline: A compilation uncovers Beirut’s music during wartime
content.standfirst: Habibi Funk’s compilation gathers Lebanese soul, disco and jazz recorded during the civil war, when musicians shared work through a close-knit tape culture. Its songs hold both the pull of escape and the reality of violence.

sources.originalTitle: Beirut City Pop

segments.body: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Beirut musicians made soul, disco and jazz amid conflict and isolation. Tapes passed between friends and families, and many artists knew one another. Beirut City Pop brings together recordings from that scene, with interviews and liner notes tracing the people and conditions behind them.

segments.title: More than a sound
segments.body: The review questions the compilation’s “city pop” framing: Beirut’s private-press recordings were made under wartime conditions, far removed from the better-resourced studio culture associated with Japanese city pop. One song’s lyrics about daily car bombs, alongside its enduring love for the city, reveal the tension between escapism and lived reality.

content.headline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa turn dance-music history into a shared celebration
content.shortHeadline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa make a maximalist dance record
content.standfirst: The pair’s first collaborative full-length draws on vintage dance records, samples and an exuberant 1990s big-beat sensibility. Its most affecting moment, the review argues, comes when the duo steps away from reference and turns toward home.

sources.originalTitle: Alchemical Sisters

segments.body: Eris Drew and Octo Octa made Alchemical Sisters in a studio built in their New Hampshire cabin, weaving samples from their dance-music archive together with instruments and synthesizers. The album’s maximalist sound channels the scale and exuberance of 1990s big beat, bringing the pair’s expansive DJ instincts into their own productions.

segments.title: A record rooted in a place
segments.body: The review hears the album as a loop between musical memory and invention: its references are part of the point, not a disguise for the duo’s own style. “Song for New Hampshire” stands apart as a warm, earnest portrait of the life they have built together.

content.headline: Jess Williamson finds her voice between Texas and Los Angeles
content.shortHeadline: Jess Williamson’s country songs make room for contradiction
content.standfirst: On A Mile South of Heaven, the songwriter turns the pull between Texas and Los Angeles into intimate country music. The review hears an artist at ease with her voice, her history and the compromises that shape both places.

sources.originalTitle: A Mile South of Heaven

segments.body: Produced by Shooter Jennings, Williamson’s sixth solo album moves between country dancehall warmth and the more languorous sound of Los Angeles. Its songs draw on the singer’s shifting sense of home, allowing each place to appear through the other rather than treating the choice as a simple either-or.

segments.title: A voice that carries its history
segments.body: The review praises Williamson’s Texas inflection and sharply observed writing, hearing a new depth in her delivery. Her songs revisit longing, regret and the desire to leave, but their central movement is toward facing those feelings rather than outrunning them.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s expanded debut reveals the work behind the breakthrough
content.shortHeadline: A Costello box set traces the making of My Aim Is True
content.standfirst: A 104-track anniversary edition follows Costello from early demos to the emergence of the artist behind My Aim Is True. The review finds a gradual process of craft and reinvention beneath the familiar story of sudden arrival.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The expanded My Aim Is True set includes demos, live recordings and material from Costello’s early years. Rather than presenting the 1977 debut as an instant, fully formed breakthrough, the collection traces a songwriter working through influences and refining his voice.

segments.title: From craftsman to agitator
segments.body: Early recordings reveal an accomplished writer drawing on American roots and singer-songwriters, before Stiff Records and collaborators helped shape the more confrontational persona associated with Costello. The review finds the demos illuminating, while judging some of the later live material more for dedicated fans than newcomers.

content.headline: Native James fuses grime and metal with a distinctly Black British voice
content.shortHeadline: Native James makes grime-metal feel gloriously unruly
content.standfirst: The Ipswich rapper threads first-wave grime, nu-metal riffs and sharp humour into a sound of his own. A recent award and festival appearances suggest a rising profile, while his next single is due at the end of October.

image.caption: Native James, the Ipswich rapper blending grime and metal.

sources.originalTitle: Add to playlist: the gloriously boisterous grime-metal of Native James and the week’s best new tracks

segments.body: Native James, whose real name is Aaron James, grew up with Evanescence and first-wave grime. His music brings rapid-fire bars together with heavy riffs, Jamaican Patois and playful references, turning the mix into what the Guardian describes as a distinctly Black British take on rap-rock.

segments.title: A sound gaining momentum
segments.body: His recent work includes the EP Confessions of a Sinner and the single Never Been Scared, which features Frisco. After a Glastonbury set and a One to Watch award at the Independent Music Awards, James is due to release Dumb Bruddah on 30 October.

content.headline: A fisherman’s fight for answers after a mass die-off reaches the screen
content.shortHeadline: A Teesside fisherman pursues answers after the sea life dies
content.standfirst: Jeanie Finlay follows Stan Rennie and other Teesside fishers after thousands of crabs washed ashore in 2021. The documentary records their search for answers without claiming to settle the disputed cause of the die-off.

image.caption: Fisherman Stan Rennie aboard his boat in Hartlepool.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seas

segments.body: In 2021, dead and dying crustaceans washed up along the Yorkshire and north-east coast. The cause remains disputed: authorities cited an algal bloom and later a pathogen, while local fishers and others questioned whether dredging near the Tees estuary was connected. Finlay’s film follows Rennie over four years as he campaigns for answers.

segments.title: A community living with the consequences
segments.body: The documentary focuses on the fishers, scientists and campaigners affected by the losses, not on proving what killed the marine life. Rennie’s collective is raising money for further testing; the film has helped bring attention to their efforts, while the Tees Valley mayor has denied allegations of wrongdoing made by some fishers.

perspectives.body: Finlay says she cannot offer an easy answer or an official cause. Her aim is to show what uncertainty and the loss of a livelihood have felt like for people who live and work on the coast.

content.headline: Lee Chang-dong asks who has the right to tell stories of working people
content.shortHeadline: Lee Chang-dong on class, capital and the ethics of filming
content.standfirst: Possible Love places a story of redundancy and wealth beside questions about documentary filmmaking and the power of the camera. Lee discusses the project’s origins and why he sees dignity in fighting an apparently unwinnable system.

image.caption: Lee Chang-dong, director of Possible Love.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender

segments.body: Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love grew from the 2009 Ssangyong Motors strike, when workers occupied a factory after mass layoffs were proposed. The film follows a working-class couple drawn into a wealthy woman’s documentary project, making labour, capital and the filmmaker’s relationship to her subjects part of the same story.

segments.title: The power behind the camera
segments.body: Lee says he struggled with whether he was entitled to tell the workers’ story, and how close he should stand to them. The film explores that uncertainty through the documentary-maker character: even without intending to, the person holding a camera has power over the person being filmed.

perspectives.body: Lee describes the characters’ struggle against capital as an “impossible fight” that can still restore dignity. He also connects their vulnerability to his own dependence on funding to make films while trying to protect his voice.

content.headline: Bond screen tests are reported, but the next 007 is still unconfirmed
content.shortHeadline: Bond finalists reportedly face screen tests this week
content.standfirst: Reports say Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor are among actors testing for the role, with accounts differing on whether three or as many as five are involved. Amazon has not confirmed the casting details.

sources.originalTitle: I expect you to cry: what the James Bond actors may face at the final audition
James Bond finalists to screen-test for role this week – reports

segments.body: The Hollywood Reporter and Variety report that a small group of actors are screen-testing in London for the next James Bond film. Callum Turner and Jack Lowden are named among those in the mix; the Guardian’s report also identifies Josh O’Connor. The reports say the tests involve stunts, camera presence and dialogue.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s accompanying commentary treats the reported tests as a long-awaited stage in the search, but its assessments of the actors’ suitability are explicitly speculation, not casting information.

segments.body: The number of finalists is unclear, and Amazon MGM has declined to comment on specific details of the casting process. Denis Villeneuve is set to direct, with Steven Knight writing the script; no actor has been officially announced.

content.headline: Sandra Hüller on East Germany, political grief and a year of films
content.shortHeadline: Sandra Hüller on politics, fame and the roles arriving together
content.standfirst: The actor discusses Fatherland’s East German perspective, the risks of political complacency and a year in which several very different films arrive at once. She says the clustering of releases is not something she controls.

image.caption: Sandra Hüller, who stars in Fatherland.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films

segments.body: Hüller says Fatherland gave space to a political idea from East Germany that did not survive reunification, and that the film’s grief feels clearer from the East. She connects its historical setting to present-day politics, warning that fascism can arrive gradually rather than all at once.

segments.title: A varied year, not a planned image
segments.body: With Fatherland, Rose, Digger and Project Hail Mary arriving in the same year, Hüller says the apparent surge is a matter of release timing, not a deliberate career plan. She also discusses her reluctance to be treated as more important than an ensemble and her work directing plays with her theatre collective.

content.headline: Junk’s two stories never quite become one film
content.shortHeadline: Junk is visually striking but never coheres
content.standfirst: David Schwimmer and two young drifters anchor a Los Angeles film that shifts between Hollywood satire and a drug-fuelled odyssey. The review admires its visual flair but finds its divided tone hard to reconcile.

image.caption: David Schwimmer in Junk.

sources.originalTitle: Junk review – David Schwimmer is lost in Mubi’s frustrating LA-set misstep

segments.body: Junk begins with a screenwriter, played by Schwimmer, caught in self-important industry talk, then pivots to two young people whose plans unravel after a robbery. Director Jack Begert finds vivid, seedy beauty in Los Angeles, but the film’s two loosely connected strands do not settle into a convincing whole.

segments.title: Ambition without a sure footing
segments.body: The review finds more life in the restless night-time sections with Dominic Fike and Talia Ryder than in the screenwriter’s self-loathing fantasies. It credits the film’s visual invention, while arguing that its meta jokes and uneven tone make the 110-minute result a frustrating misstep.

content.headline: Wildwood brings old-fashioned stop-motion magic to a forest quest
content.shortHeadline: Wildwood offers a warmly made stop-motion adventure
content.standfirst: Laika’s fantasy sends two children into a hidden wilderness of talking animals and strange rulers after a baby is carried off by crows. The review enjoys its crafted animation and earnest quest, while finding less menace than in Coraline.

image.caption: Prue enters the Wildwood in Laika’s stop-motion adventure.

sources.originalTitle: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey

segments.body: Prue and her friend Curtis follow a murder of crows into the Wildwood after they carry away her baby brother. There they find a parallel world of creatures and oppressed people, ruled by a scheming governess. The film turns Carson Ellis and Colin Meloy’s book into a direct, exuberant stop-motion adventure.

The review praises the physical immediacy of Laika’s animation and the film’s old-fashioned sense of a children’s quest. It is less convinced by the explanation for the governess’s plan and says the story lacks the unsettling force of Coraline, apart from its opening sequence.

content.headline: Lucasfilm needs to let a new Star Wars film actually get made
content.shortHeadline: Star Wars needs fewer announcements and more films
content.standfirst: Taika Waititi says his proposed Star Wars film has been put on ice, joining a long list of announced projects that never reached cinemas. The Guardian argues that the franchise must accept creative risk rather than retreat to familiar choices.

image.caption: Taika Waititi, whose proposed Star Wars film has been put on ice.

sources.originalTitle: Taika Waititi’s Star Wars film is the latest to hit the buffers. At some point Lucasfilm is going to have to actually make a movie

segments.body: Waititi’s Star Wars project, announced six years ago, has stalled, adding to proposed films from other directors that have not materialised. Since 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker, only one Star Wars film has reached cinemas, despite repeated announcements of new projects.

segments.title: The risk of playing safe
segments.body: The Guardian’s argument is that Lucasfilm should give distinctive filmmakers room to make something that might fail, rather than continually returning to familiar characters and established formulas. The piece questions whether the franchise’s caution is helping it, given the mixed reception to its recent theatrical return.

content.headline: Eight films to watch in November, from Elsinore to The Hunger Games
content.shortHeadline: What to watch in November: eight films to look out for
content.standfirst: The month’s cinema and streaming releases range from Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson to a new Hunger Games prequel and a David Fincher-directed Cliff Booth spin-off. This guide gathers dates, premises and early critical reactions.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: Among November’s releases are Elsinore, about Ian Charleson’s final stage role as Hamlet; The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, scripted by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher; and Sunrise on the Reaping, a Hunger Games prequel. The guide also covers new dramas, comedies and animation.

Release dates differ by country and platform, and several titles arrive in cinemas before streaming. The selections include films with reported awards momentum as well as commercial franchises, giving readers a practical look ahead rather than a single prediction about what will define the month.

content.headline: The Narco Hack turns an encrypted-phone investigation into gripping TV
content.shortHeadline: The Narco Hack: police break into a criminal network’s phones
content.standfirst: This three-part documentary follows French, Belgian and Dutch police as they compromised the encrypted Sky ECC app and traced organised crime. Its account of the investigation also raises questions about how technology companies respond to the people using their products.

image.caption: The Narco Hack examines a police investigation into encrypted phones.

sources.originalTitle: The Narco Hack review – an epic tale of how detectives’ tech wizardry smashed a billion-euro drugs ring

segments.body: The Narco Hack reconstructs how police undermined Sky ECC, an encrypted-phone service used by criminal networks. Investigators had to decide how long to monitor messages before acting, balancing the possibility of reaching major figures against the danger of allowing violence to continue.

segments.title: A human cost behind the data
segments.body: The investigation uncovered extreme violence and billions of euros in criminal proceeds. The documentary also shows the value of the material in clearing the name of Houcine Hakkar, who was killed after being wrongly suspected. Its account prompts broader questions about responsibility when technology finds criminal users.

perspectives.body: The review stresses that the police operation was not only a technical success: the messages surrounding Hakkar’s death answered accusations against him, offering his family a measure of truth after his murder.

content.headline: How The Traitors grew from a Dutch idea into a global television hit
content.shortHeadline: Inside the making of The Traitors
content.standfirst: The show’s creators and Claudia Winkleman explain how a game of trust and treachery became a lavish, internationally successful format. They credit its rules, setting and hands-off approach to gameplay as central to its appeal.

image.caption: Claudia Winkleman, host of The Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I always think my head will fall off when Traitors turn on each other’: the inside story of the world’s biggest TV show

segments.body: The Traitors began with a Dutch producer’s idea for a reality game inspired by the 1628 Batavia shipwreck and its survivors’ conflicts. After early versions were reshaped, the format moved from a boat to a castle, with Studio Lambert adapting and expanding it for British and American audiences.

segments.title: Letting the game unfold
segments.body: The producers say the show works because contestants play within a self-contained game, with limited intervention from the production team. Winkleman describes learning to take a stricter role as host, while the creators point to the audience’s knowledge of the Traitors as a source of suspense and comedy.

perspectives.body: Winkleman says she initially struggled with appearing cold to contestants, whom she feels protective of. She credits the producers’ guidance with helping her inhabit the role of the castle’s stern, game-focused host.

content.headline: Last One Laughing: Halloween proves the comedy format has more life
content.shortHeadline: Last One Laughing’s Halloween special is still a treat
content.standfirst: The spooky spin-off adds a no-screaming rule to the comedians’ familiar challenge, but the new twist rarely matters. The review finds the cast’s performances and spontaneous exchanges funny enough to justify another return.

image.caption: The comedians competing in Last One Laughing: Halloween.

sources.originalTitle: Last One Laughing: Halloween review – still a total treat, despite the new twist

segments.body: The Halloween edition brings seven comedians together and asks them not to laugh—or scream—while trying to make one another break. The review is initially wary of a shorter spin-off so soon after the main series, and finds the extra rule largely irrelevant in the first three episodes.

The cast’s prepared routines and improvised exchanges make the special work anyway. Reece Shearsmith’s horror tricks, Tom Allen’s asides and Jack Dee’s unusually cheerful presence all earn praise; the reviewer concludes that the format still has plenty of comic life.

content.headline: Lupin returns with bigger heists and questions about race and infamy
content.shortHeadline: Lupin raises the stakes for Assane Diop
content.standfirst: The French hit returns with Assane Diop in prison and under suspicion after new heists are announced in his name. The review links the show’s disguise-driven thrills to its treatment of race, fame and the difficulty of leaving a notorious identity behind.

image.caption: Omar Sy as Assane Diop in Lupin.

sources.originalTitle: Lupin review – the French super-thief is magnetic in his blockbuster return

segments.body: The fourth series begins with Diop in a high-security prison, weeks from release, when Paris is hit by a cyberattack and warnings of further “Lupin” heists. The review notes the unexpected resonance of the premise after the real Louvre robbery in 2025, in which thieves posed as construction workers.

segments.title: The cost of being known
segments.body: Diop’s Blackness has helped him disguise himself as a worker in previous crimes, but the same racialised assumptions become a liability once he is suspected. The review finds the new season’s twists and set pieces compelling, while asking whether the larger, more cinematic approach can retain the character’s complexity.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ cautious turret is draining the game of mischief
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors needs bolder players
content.standfirst: A review argues that several casting and gameplay choices have left this year’s Traitors without the daring that powers the format. It singles out James Acaster’s refusal to take part in a mission and Maya Jama’s polished play as problems for the show’s drama.

sources.originalTitle: Claudia picked the wrong Traitors

segments.body: The i Paper’s critique is that this celebrity series has repeatedly lost promising Traitors early, then left the remaining players too cautious. In a mission requiring the Traitors to steal pieces from Faithfuls’ shields, Acaster avoided the task, and the team failed to win money or create much tension.

The writer also finds Jama’s socially polished approach less entertaining than the vulnerability the show’s audience wants to watch. Kenny’s unexpected energy is the exception; the article argues that the remaining Traitors need to take more risks if the series is to regain its mischievous momentum.

content.headline: Isy Suttie on Taskmaster, Peep Show and finding room to write
content.shortHeadline: Isy Suttie on Taskmaster and the work she wants to make
content.standfirst: The comedian and actor talks about the freedom of being thrown into Taskmaster’s unknown, the lasting comfort viewers find in Peep Show and how parenting has changed her songwriting. She is now drawn to writing about power and control.

image.caption: Isy Suttie, who appears in the current series of Taskmaster.

sources.originalTitle: Peep Show’s Isy Suttie: ‘I muted a part of myself since having kids’

segments.body: Suttie says Taskmaster brought back a sense of uncertainty she felt had quietened as she grew older and became a parent. The show’s baffling tasks made her rely on instinct, a quality she enjoyed rediscovering alongside fellow contestants Matt Lucas, Richard Ayoade, Chloe Petts and Nina Conti.

segments.title: The work that stays with people
segments.body: Best known to many as Dobby in Peep Show, Suttie says fans tell her the series helped them through difficult periods. She recognises the same comfort in her own repeated viewing of The Inbetweeners during grief, and reflects on how having children has left less room for the unusual mental state she associates with songwriting.

content.headline: Strictly’s themed weeks are crowding out the transformation that matters
content.shortHeadline: Strictly should give its themed weeks a rest
content.standfirst: The i Paper argues that costumes and novelty themes are arriving too often this year, distracting from the celebrities’ effort to learn ballroom and Latin dance. The critique is not a call for purism, but for the show to trust its central appeal.

image.caption: Dianne Buswell and Will Best perform during Strictly’s Icons Week.

sources.originalTitle: Strictly needs to calm down – and give the fancy-dress themed weeks a rest

segments.body: Strictly’s early live shows have included both Movies Week and Icons Week, with Halloween still to come. The writer says the compressed run of themed nights makes costumes, sketches and extra gags feel like an attempt to hold attention rather than let the dancers’ progress carry the series.

The argument is not that Strictly should be a ballroom purist’s competition. Its appeal lies in watching celebrities take on a new skill, grow more confident and build partnerships over time. The writer says themed dressing works best as an occasional break from that progression, not as a substitute for it.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream, from Nocturne to a Matthew Perry documentary
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream this week
content.standfirst: This week’s picks include Stephen Graham in a prison-set thriller, a documentary about Matthew Perry and a new darts competition. The guide also flags returning franchises and the limits of another Dexter revival.

image.caption: Stephen Graham in Nocturne.

sources.originalTitle: Nocturne to The One About Matthew Perry: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Guardian’s selection ranges from Nocturne, a thriller led by Stephen Graham, to The One About Matthew Perry, a three-part documentary described as both affectionate and candid about the actor’s troubles. Other recommendations include a low-budget pizzeria mockumentary and a darts contest built around a challenge to Luke Littler.

The guide is not uniformly enthusiastic: it finds Dexter’s latest return familiar and non-essential, while noting the unfinished-feeling trajectory of another horror anthology. Release dates and platforms are given for each selection, making this a practical watchlist as well as a set of recommendations.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans grieving a studio’s legacy
content.shortHeadline: BioWare closes, ending hopes for its next Mass Effect
content.standfirst: The writer reflects on EA’s reported closure of BioWare, the cancellation of a new Mass Effect and the loss of more than 400 jobs. The studio’s choice-driven role-playing games, they argue, leave a lasting mark on the genre.

image.caption: Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s science-fiction role-playing series.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The Guardian’s writer, a longtime BioWare fan and games-industry worker, says EA’s closure of the studio has ended work on a new Mass Effect and put more than 400 jobs at risk. The piece connects the decision to the studio’s recent lack of major hits and EA’s debt after a leveraged buyout.

segments.title: The story players made their own
segments.body: The writer recalls how Mass Effect’s characters, moral choices and consequences made the trilogy feel personal, with decisions carrying across games. Though BioWare’s recent years included missteps, the loss of a studio associated with influential, character-led role-playing games feels especially final to fans.

perspectives.body: The author’s account is both industry reflection and personal testimony: they describe returning to the first Mass Effect after initially giving up, then replaying the trilogy for years because of its characters and consequential choices.

content.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a glossy, globe-spanning thrill ride
content.shortHeadline: Modern Warfare 4 throws everything at its campaign
content.standfirst: The latest Call of Duty campaign races from Manhattan rooftops to a North Korean airbase, with multiplayer and an expanded extraction mode alongside it. The review praises the spectacle but notes the short campaign and the franchise’s militarised fantasy.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

sources.originalTitle: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game

segments.body: Modern Warfare 4’s six-hour campaign centres on a fictional North Korean invasion of the South and mixes familiar Call of Duty set pieces with an open-world section. The review calls it a fast-moving, polished experience, though it finds Mads Mikkelsen’s antagonist underused and Captain Price’s ending less affecting than intended.

segments.title: More than the campaign
segments.body: The review finds the multiplayer familiar but refined, while the rebuilt DMZ extraction mode offers a larger world, missions and upgrades. Its success remains uncertain because the reviewer has only played an early-access version; the piece also questions the series’ glossy treatment of armed conflict.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, unsettling game
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony explores Antarctica through a penguin’s eyes
content.standfirst: This semi-open adventure sends players waddling through a frozen landscape populated by Nazis, old expedition records and Lovecraftian horrors. Its odd perspective becomes a way to challenge human arrogance and invite a different kind of exploration.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Players guide penguins across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity, switching between birds with different abilities and collecting words rather than conventional prizes. The review describes a world that shifts from simple ice fields to labyrinths, obelisks and crevasses, rendered in jagged, low-poly graphics.

segments.title: A perspective outside the human story
segments.body: A narrator recounts an earlier expedition as the game layers archival footage, Nazi delusion and unsettling discoveries into the penguins’ journey. Despite some control and audio glitches, the review finds the ending a forceful rejection of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism, and a prompt to explore without human certainty.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time’s Switch 2 remake asks what a classic should look like now
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time faces its 4K remake
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s remake adds modern controls and a newly orchestrated score to a game first released in 1998. The preview weighs the smoother play against a more contentious makeover of Link and the challenge of revisiting a defining classic.

image.caption: Link in the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time gives Link a sprint, manual jump, free camera and easier-to-use inventory, while making Hyrule more detailed. The preview finds the controls strikingly different from the N64 original, even as the familiar dungeons and puzzles retain their appeal.

segments.title: How far should a remake go?
segments.body: The new orchestral soundtrack impresses, but Link’s glossy, wide-eyed design has drawn criticism as technological polish for its own sake. The preview considers an alternative interpretation: the character may reflect Japanese puppet traditions, making his stylised appearance a deliberate artistic choice rather than a simple upgrade.

perspectives.body: A Japanese games veteran and a writer on Japanese culture offer a possible context for Link’s doll-like design, but the preview stresses that Nintendo has not explained its intent.

content.headline: Switch Sports Resort makes family play feel like a holiday
content.shortHeadline: Switch Sports Resort brings the family together
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s sequel combines familiar sports with new events and a resort to explore. The review finds it easy to pick up with others, while its small touches of atmosphere give solo play more to discover.

image.caption: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings its sports to a lively island setting.

sources.originalTitle: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games

segments.body: Switch Sports Resort brings back tennis, bowling and volleyball, adds golf and basketball, and introduces seven more activities including archery, skateboarding and jetskiing. The reviewer finds the sports intuitive and playful, though basketball’s turn-taking feels less like the fast-paced real game.

segments.title: A place to come back to
segments.body: The resort’s beaches, cafes and tiny visitors give the collection a sense of place, while unlockable outfits and sport variations provide reasons to keep playing alone. The reviewer’s family has made the game a fixture, with enough variety to engage both younger players and visiting friends.

content.headline: Modern Warfare 4 puts character and consequence inside the action
content.shortHeadline: How Modern Warfare 4 ties its battles to character
content.standfirst: Infinity Ward’s narrative director explains how the game connects a South Korean soldier’s unit with Captain Price’s pursuit of Makarov. The developers say military and cultural consultants helped them make the fictional conflict feel grounded.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines combat with character-led storytelling.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon

segments.body: Modern Warfare 4’s story moves between a young South Korean conscript caught in an invasion and Captain Price’s morally ambiguous hunt for Makarov. Narrative director Jeff Negus says the team began by asking whether the story felt plausible and what might resonate with players.

segments.title: Action with a human stake
segments.body: Negus says the developers aimed to connect quieter character scenes with large battles so that the action would matter to the people caught in it. The team consulted military specialists and Korean actors, alongside a dialect coach, on details of the setting and language.

perspectives.body: Negus describes the goal as “player-protagonist parity”: players should feel what the characters feel, so that action mechanics and narrative become parts of the same story.

content.headline: Personalised mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk in phase III trial
content.shortHeadline: Personalised vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk
content.standfirst: In a trial of 1,137 people whose melanoma had been removed, adding an individualised mRNA vaccine to pembrolizumab reduced the two-year risk of recurrence or death by 42% compared with the drug alone.

image.caption: Prof Georgina Long, medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows

segments.body: The Australian-led phase III trial compared pembrolizumab alone with the same treatment combined with intismeran, a vaccine tailored to mutations in each person’s melanoma. At two years, 82% of people given the combination were alive and recurrence-free, compared with 70% of those given pembrolizumab alone.

segments.title: What the results do — and don’t — show
segments.body: The results have been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and are still to undergo peer review. The manufacturers say it is too early to determine whether the combination improves long-term survival. The vaccine is not yet a standard treatment and would require further study and regulatory review.

The researchers and outside experts point to important limits: some patients do not respond, and cancer can adapt to treatment. Further research is also needed to establish whether the approach could help people with visible cancer or those who do not respond to pembrolizumab.

content.headline: India caps mark-ups on 137 cancer drugs after court condemns prices
content.shortHeadline: India caps mark-ups on 137 cancer drugs
content.standfirst: A 30% trade-margin cap is being extended to 137 cancer medicines after India’s supreme court criticised steep mark-ups. The government expects prices to fall by as much as 70%, though campaigners warn broader supply-chain reform is needed.

image.caption: Cancer medicines in India are expected to become cheaper under a new price cap.

sources.originalTitle: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’

segments.body: From next month, India will apply a 30% cap on trade margins to 137 additional cancer drugs. The move follows a court case brought by Sarojam Radhakrishnan, who could not afford prescribed breast-cancer medicines. The supreme court described some mark-ups as “extortion” and noted that a drug supplied to hospitals for 2,700 rupees was priced at 27,000.

segments.title: Access beyond the price cap
segments.body: The Department of Pharmaceuticals expects the measure to reduce prices by up to 70%. Oncologists and advocates welcome a step that could help patients continue treatment, but warn that families still face high medical costs. A civil-society representative also cautions that hospitals could seek to recover lost revenue through other charges; the court has asked the government why the cap should not apply to other non-patented medicines.

content.headline: Optogenetics restores some vision in a small trial, with wider uses in view
content.shortHeadline: Light-based gene therapy restores some vision
content.standfirst: Six of 10 patients with advanced retinitis pigmentosa gained useful vision in one eye after gene therapy made retinal cells respond to amber light. The approach is experimental, and other proposed uses remain at earlier stages.

image.caption: Optogenetics uses light to control nerve-cell activity.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: In a study of 10 patients with retinitis pigmentosa, a gene therapy enabled cells in the retina to respond to amber light. After three months, six participants had meaningfully improved vision in the treated eye, including being able to pick up a cup from a table. They wore special glasses and had to learn to interpret the new visual signals.

segments.title: A precise tool, still under development
segments.body: Optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control nerve-cell activity. It offers researchers a way to target cells more precisely than electrical stimulation, and may have applications in conditions involving nerves. But the vision treatment does not restore normal sight: participants could not distinguish faces, and the technique is still progressing cautiously from research towards clinical use.

Potential treatments for pain and epilepsy are being investigated, while optogenetic hearing technology remains at the animal-testing stage. Some approaches would require gene therapy that may be irreversible, making safety evidence essential before wider use.

content.headline: UK flu season starts early, but that does not mean a worse winter
content.shortHeadline: Early flu rise is no guarantee of a worse season
content.standfirst: Flu infections in the UK are rising earlier than usual, prompting health officials to urge eligible people to get vaccinated. Researchers say the timing alone cannot predict how severe the season will be.

image.caption: Respiratory viruses are appearing earlier in the UK this autumn.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: Flu activity is rising in the UK in October, earlier than the usual December or January peak. The timing varies from year to year, and experts say an early start does not necessarily mean more infections or deaths overall. Last year’s season also began early but ended with fewer flu deaths than average.

segments.title: What may be driving the shift
segments.body: Possible factors include changes in circulating flu strains and the timing of the southern hemisphere’s flu season, which can influence which viruses reach the UK. Cold, dry air and more time spent indoors may also help explain why respiratory viruses tend to spread in winter. It remains uncertain which factors best explain this year’s early rise.

Flu often comes on quickly, with fever, shivering and muscle aches; colds more commonly bring a runny nose, sneezing, cough and sore throat. The UK Health Security Agency is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to take it up promptly.

content.headline: Drought-tolerant crops could reshape what UK farmers grow
content.shortHeadline: Hotter summers put new crops on the UK menu
content.standfirst: After a hot, dry summer damaged harvests, researchers are testing crops such as lupins and chickpeas that may cope better with warmer conditions. Their suitability for UK farms still needs careful testing.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with flour from a potentially drought-tolerant crop.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: A government-funded research network is investigating how UK crops may need to change as summers become hotter and drier. Lupins and chickpeas are among the crops being assessed for their drought tolerance, while researchers are working with chefs and food businesses to explore how they might be used.

segments.title: Testing before scaling up
segments.body: Lupin flour is higher in protein and lower in starch than wheat flour, but edible varieties are different from ornamental garden lupins and require appropriate processing. Researchers say chickpeas also need further work on which varieties and locations are suitable, and on possible pests and diseases. The aim is to establish the evidence before farmers commit to large-scale planting.

A warmer climate could also shift where familiar crops grow best, but the changes are not straightforward: late spring frosts may still damage fruit blossom. Researchers and horticultural advisers say the winners and losers for UK growers remain difficult to predict.

content.headline: Biodiversity fund has received just $7,085 from major drugmakers
content.shortHeadline: Biodiversity fund remains nearly empty
content.standfirst: The Cali Fund aims to raise $1bn a year from businesses that benefit from genetic information in nature, but just $7,085 has been deposited. Drugmakers question the voluntary scheme’s design as biodiversity talks resume.

image.caption: Genetic information from nature can contribute to medical research.

sources.originalTitle: Big pharma accused of ‘free-riding on nature’ as global fund attracts just $7,000

segments.body: The Cali Fund had received $10,656 in commitments by the start of the Cop17 biodiversity summit in Armenia, with $7,085 deposited. It was created to channel contributions from businesses that benefit from digital genetic information towards conservation, including in low-income countries and areas identified as priorities by Indigenous peoples and local communities.

segments.title: Dispute over how contributions should work
segments.body: No major pharmaceutical company has contributed. Industry representatives argue that the proposed voluntary payments do not reflect whether digital sequence information was used in a particular medicine and may overlap with existing rules. Conservation advocates say voluntary contributions are unlikely to meet the fund’s ambitions, while the fund’s organisers say payments may grow as its operating arrangements are completed.

content.headline: CoastSnap turns phone photos into a record of changing shorelines
content.shortHeadline: Citizen photos help track changing coastlines
content.standfirst: A fixed phone cradle and an app let volunteers photograph the same stretch of beach over time. Researchers use the images to monitor erosion, storm impacts and the results of beach-replenishment projects.

image.caption: Praa Sands in Cornwall, one of the coastlines monitored by citizen scientists.

sources.originalTitle: How citizen science is tracking changes in shorelines around the world
