segments.body: CoastSnap began in Australia in 2017 and now has more than 200 stations in 21 countries. Volunteers place a phone in a cradle to take photographs from a consistent position and send the images to researchers, creating a record of how coastlines change.

Software aligns the photographs, transforms them into a bird’s-eye view and maps the shoreline while accounting for the tide using the image’s timestamp. The resulting records can help researchers track longer-term erosion, examine the effects of a particular storm or assess beach-replenishment schemes.

content.headline: Archaeologist suggests Westminster Abbey sarcophagus held an abbot
content.shortHeadline: Roman coffin may hold a medieval abbot
content.standfirst: Radiocarbon dating places the skeleton in a reused Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey in the late 10th or early 11th century. An archaeologist argues the burial was probably an abbot, but the person’s identity is not certain.

image.caption: The Roman sarcophagus on display in Westminster Abbey’s Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

sources.originalTitle: Mystery of Roman sarcophagus unearthed at Westminster Abbey solved at last, expert says

segments.body: The limestone sarcophagus, inscribed with the Roman name Valerius Amandinus, contained a man’s skeleton when its lid was removed for study in 2018. Radiocarbon dating places the bones in the late 10th or early 11th century, centuries after the sarcophagus itself was made.

Westminster Abbey archaeologist Warwick Rodwell believes the elaborate burial was most likely for an abbot, with Ælfwig a stronger candidate than Wulfnoth. The remains have not been definitively identified; the conclusion is an interpretation based on the dating, the modified lid and the status suggested by the burial.

content.headline: PHP flaws trigger global patching scramble, but successful attacks remain unpro
content.shortHeadline: PHP flaw sparks global scramble; confirmed damage unclear
content.standfirst: Long-hidden PHP vulnerabilities prompted organisations to patch or take websites offline as reports of exploitation attempts surged. Authorities and researchers say no large-scale breach has been confirmed, but some consequences may take time to emerge.

image.caption: A BBC webpage temporarily unavailable during the PHP security response.

sources.originalTitle: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber-security scramble
Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb
What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber-security scramble

segments.body: Two severe flaws in PHP, a programming language used by many websites and other systems, could let attackers run code on affected servers. Governments and companies took services offline or applied fixes. The UK said 32 government services had been taken offline as a precaution; officials said that did not mean they had been hacked.

segments.title: Attempts, reports and what remains unknown
segments.body: Cloudflare reported millions of attempts to exploit the flaws, while Amazon said it had seen attempts and that its websites were operating normally. A separate BBC account said Amazon had identified an attempt against a decoy system before the warning became public. Reports of attempts are not proof of successful compromise; security researchers and authorities had no confirmed large-scale breach to report, and any impact could take time to become clear.

The PHP Foundation issued patches, but older systems may need upgrading before they can be fixed. Website owners are urged to check with their hosting provider or developer that PHP itself has been patched; updating WordPress or its plugins alone will not resolve the underlying issue. IT workers also described long hours and misleading reports of working attacks, raising concern about alert fatigue.

content.headline: Quest Diagnostics says cyberattack exposed some patient records
content.shortHeadline: Quest says cyberattack exposed patient records
content.standfirst: The US laboratory company says attackers accessed patient information held in its Quanum system, which supports testing and billing for healthcare providers. Quest has not said how many people were affected or what specific records were taken.

sources.originalTitle: Lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics confirms patients’ personal and health data was compromised during breach

segments.body: Quest Diagnostics disclosed that an attacker gained unauthorised access to Quanum, a system used by doctors’ offices, hospitals and other healthcare providers to order tests and handle billing. The company says the access included “certain patient records” and that it has notified law enforcement and is investigating.

segments.title: Scale and data not yet known
segments.body: Quest has not said when the breach began, how many patients or healthcare customers were affected, or which kinds of personal and medical information were taken. Quanum is used by about half a million clinicians, but the number of records held in the system is unclear. The disclosure adds to a series of cyber incidents affecting healthcare companies.

content.headline: AI firms urge UK to share more benefits with communities hosting data centres
content.shortHeadline: AI firms seek local benefits to head off data-centre protests
content.standfirst: A taskforce including Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco says the UK has about a year to build public support for data-centre projects. Critics argue that financial incentives will not address concerns over energy, water and corporate accountability.

image.caption: Protesters oppose a data-centre development in North Ayrshire.

sources.originalTitle: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened

segments.body: The Sovereign AI Leadership taskforce is urging ministers to set out how communities can benefit from hosting data centres, including through financial contributions or facilities. Its members say organised opposition has already stopped permitted projects in parts of the US and warn that similar resistance is emerging in Britain.

segments.title: Consent or compensation?
segments.body: Campaigners challenge the proposal from opposing directions. PauseAI UK says residents may see benefits as an attempt to buy consent, while Action to Protect Rural Scotland says community opposition is already well established. Foxglove argues that allowing councils to keep more business rates could shift money from central services without making data-centre companies pay more.

The UK government says data centres should provide jobs, investment and supply chains, prioritise clean power and use water responsibly. It says local planning processes consider community benefits, and that authorities in English AI growth zones can already retain additional business rates generated by the developments.

content.headline: UK plans AI wildfire unit alongside protective gear and aircraft
content.shortHeadline: UK plans AI unit to help spot wildfires
content.standfirst: The government plans an AI unit to help identify fires, £45m for specialist protective equipment and military aircraft to support crews. The proposals follow a summer of damaging blazes and questions over fire-service readiness.

image.caption: Firefighters inspect scorched scrubland near Dunwich Heath in Suffolk.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer

segments.body: The government plans to create an AI wildfire unit in the National Situation Centre to help spot and fight fires faster. At a wildfire resilience summit, businesses including Google, Airbus and VodafoneThree are expected to discuss how satellite monitoring and early-warning systems could assist the response.

segments.title: Equipment and preparedness
segments.body: The package includes £45m for specialist protective equipment and access to military aircraft for remote or difficult terrain. The announcements follow reporting that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to an information request lacked wildfire-specific protective equipment. The government also plans grants for farmers and £25m to restore peatlands in England as natural firebreaks.

The AI unit is part of a broader preparedness plan, not evidence that automated systems can replace crews or equipment. The proposals include examining local restrictions or product bans during high-risk periods, while a campaigner argues that peatland restoration funding should be followed by wider landscape recovery and duties on landowners.

content.headline: AI scammer impersonated journalist in pitch to scientific journals
content.shortHeadline: AI impersonation scam targets freelance journalist
content.standfirst: A journal published an article under Caroline Williams’s name after a suspected impersonator used her work history to pitch editors. The incident highlights how AI-assisted fraud can damage a freelancer’s reputation as well as deceive publishers.

image.caption: Journalist Caroline Williams says a suspected impersonation scam put her reputation at risk.

sources.originalTitle: My identity was stolen by an AI scammer. It could happen to anyone

segments.body: Freelance journalist Caroline Williams discovered that Science had published an article under her name which she had not written. Editors said the story had been pitched by someone else, contained copied quotations and was flagged by AI-detection software. The journal removed it after learning of the suspected deception.

segments.title: A disputed identity
segments.body: The person who submitted the article denied impersonating Williams, saying the piece was their own work. But editors told the paper the pitch identified the writer as the UK journalist, and the pitch linked to Williams’s earlier work. Science says it will speak with new writers by phone or video and use AI-detection tools.

Williams says the episode threatens the reputation and relationships on which freelance work depends. She also warns that poorly written or inaccurate AI-generated articles, especially those involving health, could mislead readers if treated as reliable reporting.

content.headline: AI tools help TV owners remove ads, but privacy fixes have limits
content.shortHeadline: AI-assisted TV tweaks target ads and tracking
content.standfirst: Owners of some Android and Google TV sets are using AI-assisted projects to simplify menus, block some tracking and remove ads. The changes rely on existing developer tools, may not stop all data collection and can damage a device if misused.

sources.originalTitle: People are vibe coding their way to better TVs

segments.body: New community projects use Android’s built-in developer tools to remove some sponsored content, disable selected packages and install simpler TV launchers. Some users are using coding assistants to customise those interfaces. The underlying tools predate the AI trend; AI has made it quicker for people to apply or adapt them.

segments.title: Not a complete privacy fix
segments.body: The projects mainly target Android and Google TV sets, and do not offer the same approach for some other television operating systems. Blocking selected internet addresses cannot reveal all data sent by a connected TV, particularly when traffic is encrypted. Manufacturers’ viewing-data features may be turned off in settings, though the controls can be difficult to find.

Changing settings with developer tools can carry risks: one user reported bricking a Samsung television. The reporting argues that the projects’ popularity is also a warning to manufacturers about frustration with advertising, tracking and cluttered interfaces.

content.headline: Oura sues Ultrahuman again, seeking to block US Ring Pro sales
content.shortHeadline: Oura lawsuit threatens Ultrahuman’s US ring sales
content.standfirst: Oura alleges that Ultrahuman’s redesigned Ring Pro infringes two patents and is seeking damages and a sales injunction. Ultrahuman denies the claims and says the ring remains available while the dispute proceeds.

image.caption: Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro, at the centre of a new patent lawsuit.

sources.originalTitle: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback

segments.body: Oura has filed a new patent lawsuit against Ultrahuman, alleging that the Ring Pro infringes patents covering its design and internal components. One of the patents was issued two days before the lawsuit was filed. Oura is seeking monetary damages and an order that would stop US sales.

segments.title: A continuing patent dispute
segments.body: The companies have been in conflict since an earlier patent ruling led to an import ban on Ultrahuman’s Ring Air. Ultrahuman says a later customs ruling allowed its redesigned Ring Pro to return to the US market, and its chief executive says the company will defend itself. There is no court order affecting Ring Pro at present, he said.

content.headline: Microsoft AI beats generalist doctors on diagnostic tests, but real-world proof
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft AI beats generalist doctors in case tests
content.standfirst: Microsoft’s multi-agent system scored higher than generalist physicians on retrospective medical cases, but it has not yet been validated in clinical practice. The comparisons also leave open how much benefit comes from the orchestration system rather than the underlying models.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions
Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’

segments.body: Microsoft says its Diagnostic Orchestrator, which uses multiple AI agents to examine symptoms, consider tests and reach a diagnosis, scored about 83% on cases drawn from published medical reports. Generalist physicians using references scored about 36%, and those without them about 22%. On emergency-department cases, the system scored 80%, compared with an average of 47% for doctors in the comparison.

segments.title: A benchmark is not a clinical trial
segments.body: The evaluations used past cases rather than patients receiving care, and Microsoft says clinical validation is still needed. The comparison of complex cases was with generalist doctors, not the specialist teams that would usually handle such cases.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch’s account notes that the study’s own results show much of the improvement came from stronger underlying models. Microsoft’s orchestration added further gains in some comparisons, but those gains varied by model and type of case.

segments.body: Microsoft plans to evaluate the system with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. The company presents diagnosis as one part of a wider healthcare ambition; the effectiveness and safety of using such systems in real clinical settings remain to be established.

content.headline: Workers in India film everyday tasks to train AI for robots
content.shortHeadline: Indian workers record tasks to train robots
content.standfirst: Workers in India are paid to record activities such as tailoring, cooking and hairdressing for companies developing physical AI. The work offers extra income, while raising questions about consent, low pay and the jobs robots could eventually replace.

image.caption: A worker wears a camera to record his hands while working.

sources.originalTitle: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI

segments.body: Workers wear head-mounted cameras while doing familiar tasks so companies can collect video for training AI systems intended to control robots. The footage can show how hands and bodies move through real environments—information that robotics firms say is difficult to obtain from computer simulations alone.

segments.title: Income and consent
segments.body: One data-collection company says it pays $5 to $10 for eight to 10 hours of recorded work and blurs faces in some footage. Customers are increasingly requesting several cameras to capture more of a scene. Workers quoted in the report describe the pay as useful income, while an academic warns that people may not know how their participation could affect their future work.

The companies gather and package the footage for technology firms and research organisations. A data-business founder argues that India should build expertise beyond supplying raw video, including in processing, validation and standards. Whether robots trained on the data will replace particular jobs remains uncertain.

content.headline: Anthropic says AI reshapes its workforce, but outside experts question the claim
content.shortHeadline: Experts question Anthropic’s claims about AI and jobs
content.standfirst: Anthropic says employees now spend more time directing AI agents and that it has hired fewer junior technical workers. Researchers caution that the company’s own data does not establish that AI caused wider job losses or that its experience will predict other workplaces.

image.caption: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei at a technology conference.

sources.originalTitle: Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company

segments.body: Anthropic reports that its AI agents logged more work hours than employees from May 2026 and that staff now spend about 22% of their time managing Claude agents. It also says entry-level technical hires fell from nearly 30% to 9% of hiring since March 2025, and presents its own workplace as an example of how AI could reorganise work.

segments.title: Causation and evidence under scrutiny
segments.body: Researchers quoted in the reporting say Anthropic’s account is not an independent assessment and does not show how workers experience the changes. One researcher’s paper, which is still in peer review, finds job-market deterioration began before ChatGPT’s release. Other factors, including cuts to pandemic-era hiring and “AI-washing”, may help explain layoffs attributed to AI.

Anthropic suggests workers should share financially in successful AI adoption. A research engineer quoted in the report questions whether reducing junior hiring while asking remaining staff to manage agents is sustainable. The company did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

content.headline: AI agents on a virtual island learned through unscripted play, study finds
content.shortHeadline: Virtual-island experiment tests AI agents’ play
content.standfirst: In a preprint study, 13 AI agents explored a simulated island for 30 hours and later performed better on some challenges than agents that had not explored it. Researchers say the results suggest a possible learning approach, not proof that the systems experience play as humans do.

image.caption: A scene from the researchers’ simulated-island experiment.

sources.originalTitle: Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing

segments.body: MIT researchers left 13 AI agents on a virtual island without a specific task. The agents invented activities, including throwing objects and building structures. After the exploration period, they generally did better than comparison agents on challenges such as moving objects to a high rock spire.

segments.title: An early result, not evidence of humanlike experience
segments.body: The researchers shared their paper on arXiv, where studies are posted before peer review. The agents were prompted with a description that included being “naturally curious”; a cognitive scientist quoted in the reporting said more evidence would be needed to establish whether they were genuinely playing. The researchers frame unguided exploration as a possible way to help agents acquire useful skills.

content.headline: AI speeds up retro-game ports but strains preservation communities
content.shortHeadline: AI game ports divide retro-preservation community
content.standfirst: AI coding tools have helped hobbyists adapt classic games for new devices, but some preservationists say rushed ports can take credit from open projects and obscure how the original games were built.

sources.originalTitle: Retro gaming is being overrun with AI

segments.body: AI coding tools have accelerated hobbyist efforts to decompile and rebuild older games for platforms they were not designed for. A developer quoted by The Verge says AI made it possible to pursue more projects at once, though similar work could have been done manually with substantially more time.

segments.title: Speed versus shared knowledge
segments.body: Preservationists argue that AI-produced ports may not explain how a game’s original code works and can rely on community projects without meaningful contributions or credit. One community resource site shut down, saying that hostile AI-assisted forks had undermined the collaborative work it was built to support.

Supporters say faster tools can bring new people into game preservation and make old titles easier to access. The reporting describes a growing divide over whether speed and accessibility can be balanced with careful documentation, credit and respect for the work of existing communities.

content.headline: Meta delays disputed terms after publishers fear AI scraping rights
content.shortHeadline: Meta delays terms amid AI-scraping concerns
content.standfirst: Meta has pushed back the start date for new business terms after publishers and legal experts warned that broad language could permit scraping content for AI products. Meta says the delay will give it time to explain the changes and points to site owners’ existing controls.

sources.originalTitle: Meta delays new business terms after publisher pushback on AI scraping
Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say

segments.body: Meta says its new business terms will now take effect on November 20 rather than October 30, following objections from publishers and regulators. The company says the extra time will let it explain how it uses web crawlers and how site owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences.

segments.title: What the language could allow
segments.body: Meta removed wording that explicitly referred to using scraped material to “train” its products, but legal experts told Nieman Lab that broader language about developing business products could still encompass AI training. Meta disputes that the terms create new rights or are intended to scrape news sites.

perspectives.body: Legal experts cited by Nieman Lab say removing the word “train” may not resolve the issue: they argue that using content to “develop” a business product could still cover AI development, and that the revised language leaves important terms undefined.

content.headline: AI agents used in attacks on thousands of firms after ConnectWise breach
content.shortHeadline: AI agents accelerated attacks on ConnectWise customers
content.standfirst: Microsoft says China-aligned hackers used AI agents to make nearly 3,000 attempted sign-ins a minute against about 2,250 organisations after breaching a ConnectWise service. ConnectWise has paused access while it investigates; the reported attempts do not establish that every organisation was compromised.

sources.originalTitle: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise

segments.body: Microsoft says attackers accessed ConnectWise’s cloud backup service and stole application credentials used to connect it with customers’ systems. Those credentials could let intruders enter customer Microsoft-hosted environments and access files as if they were authorised users. Microsoft attributes the operation to China-aligned hackers.

segments.title: Speed and exposure
segments.body: Microsoft says the attackers used an open-source AI framework to conduct activity against around 2,250 organisations, at a rate of nearly 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute. ConnectWise paused access to its cloud backup service and said it was investigating and working to restore it. The report does not establish how many organisations suffered unauthorised access.

content.headline: UK AI minister says state must build its own AI capacity
content.shortHeadline: AI minister urges UK to build state capability
content.standfirst: Kanishka Narayan says the UK should not leave AI’s direction to technology companies alone, arguing for domestic capability alongside regulation. He says a government AI exercise found 500 vulnerabilities, but gave no details about the systems or findings.

sources.originalTitle: Don't leave AI to tech bros and oligarchs, UK's AI minister says

segments.body: The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, told the BBC that the public and democratic institutions should have influence over the technology, rather than leaving it to “tech bros and oligarchs”. He compared the scale of change with the Industrial Revolution and said the UK should avoid a transition that leaves too many people bearing its costs.

segments.title: Security claims without detail
segments.body: Narayan said the government spent £13,000 using frontier AI models to identify 500 novel vulnerabilities in public-sector systems. He did not identify the systems, explain the findings or say whether any had been exploited. He also argued that building AI expertise in Britain would give the country more influence over working conditions and reduce reliance on other countries for essential technology.

content.headline: Bournemouth's 3-0 win over Milan underlines Premier League's European power
content.shortHeadline: Bournemouth beat Milan 3-0 as Premier League power shows
content.standfirst: Bournemouth beat seven-time European champions AC Milan in only their third European fixture. The result also feeds a broader picture of English clubs' strength in the Europa League and Conference League.

image.caption: Bournemouth have beaten Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz and AC Milan in the Europa League.

sources.originalTitle: Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power

segments.body: Justin Kluivert opened the scoring as Bournemouth beat AC Milan 3-0 at Vitality Stadium. Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan was sent off after 27 minutes, but BBC Sport reports Bournemouth were the better side even before the dismissal.

segments.title: A wider English advantage
segments.body: The report places the win in the context of Premier League clubs' strong recent record in Europe's secondary competitions: English sides have lost just four of 26 continental matches this season. It points to greater broadcasting income, spending and wages as key advantages, while noting that this success has not translated into consistent Champions League wins.

content.headline: Brook's record 202 cannot prevent Sri Lanka's remarkable 430 chase
content.shortHeadline: Brook's record 202 ends in defeat as Sri Lanka chase 430
content.standfirst: Harry Brook made England's first ODI double-century, but Sri Lanka completed the second-highest successful chase in the format's history. England now need to win their next two matches to reach the tri-series final.

image.caption: Harry Brook hit the fastest double-century in ODI history.

sources.originalTitle: Sri Lanka make 430 to beat England after Brook's 202
Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in remarkable defeat

segments.body: Brook struck 202 from 116 balls as England made 429-4 in Rawalpindi, but Sri Lanka reached 430-8 with one ball to spare. Pavan Rathnayake made 130, while Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka each scored 97. It was the second-highest successful chase in men's ODI history.

segments.title: A record innings, a costly defeat
segments.body: England's bowling and fielding faltered in difficult conditions. Sam Curran conceded 103 runs from nine overs, and the report questions the use of the bowling options as Sri Lanka kept pace with the target. England have no wins after two tri-series matches and need to beat Pakistan in their next two games to reach the final.

perspectives.body: BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt argues that the innings further establishes Brook as a leading all-format batter. He also highlights the demands of Brook's workload and the absence of a major tournament win to match his individual milestones.

content.headline: South Africa rout Australia to level series and raise selection questions
content.shortHeadline: South Africa level series after innings win over Australia
content.standfirst: South Africa won the second Test by an innings and 31 runs, levelling the series with one match left. Australia's batting failures have put several places under scrutiny ahead of the decider.

image.caption: Australia were beaten by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha.

sources.originalTitle: What next for Australia after chastening defeat by South Africa?

segments.body: Australia were bowled out for 99 in their first innings and made 295 in their second, with Travis Head scoring 121. South Africa's 425-9 declared secured an innings-and-31-run win in Gqeberha and wiped out Australia's series lead.

segments.title: Selection under pressure
segments.body: Marnus Labuschagne has gone 47 innings without an international century, while opener Nic Maddinson's three low scores in the series have left his place in doubt. Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and Cooper Connolly are among the possible options discussed in the report. The series decider begins in Cape Town on Tuesday.

content.headline: Manchester United keep Fernandes as captain amid Carrick uncertainty
content.shortHeadline: Fernandes stays captain as United weigh Carrick's future
content.standfirst: Bruno Fernandes will not be disciplined for criticising Michael Carrick after Manchester United's 4-1 loss to Como. Carrick is expected to lead Sunday's match, but the club has begun identifying possible replacements.

image.caption: Michael Carrick apologises to Manchester United's 700 travelling fans after the defeat by Como.

sources.originalTitle: Fernandes to stay captain as Rooney calls Man Utd players babies
Carrick carrying on but senior Man Utd figures concerned by performances

segments.body: Fernandes remains Manchester United captain after questioning Carrick's tactics following the defeat by Como. The club will not discipline him. Carrick is expected to be in charge against Bournemouth on Sunday, although senior figures are concerned about results and performances.

segments.title: Responsibility under debate
segments.body: United have begun identifying possible replacements, but some at the club believe frequent managerial changes have not solved the team's decline and that underperforming players also bear responsibility. Former United striker Wayne Rooney, speaking on the United Stand podcast, called the players selfish and said they needed to take responsibility on the pitch.

perspectives.body: Rooney says Fernandes and other players risk shifting blame away from their own performances. He also urged the club's board to clarify Carrick's position and advised the head coach to stand up for himself.

content.headline: Celtic's European collapse deepens with third straight Europa League loss
content.shortHeadline: Celtic lose third straight Europa League game
content.standfirst: Celtic led Celta Vigo before conceding twice in three minutes to lose 2-1. They are 35th of 36 teams after three Europa League defeats, and criticism is growing over their ability to compete at this level.

sources.originalTitle: O'Neill bemoans marginal moments but are Celtic just not good enough?

segments.body: Mika Baur put Celtic ahead on 47 minutes, but Javi Rodriguez scored twice in three minutes as Celta Vigo won 2-1. Celtic have now lost all three of their Europa League matches and sit 35th in the 36-team table.

segments.title: Questions after another collapse
segments.body: Manager Martin O'Neill pointed to a free-kick decision and a missed chance to make it 2-0. Former Scotland attacker James McFadden said Celtic were short of the required standard, while former Celtic goalkeeper Pat Bonner questioned whether they were good enough individually and collectively. O'Neill said his side must find a way to win their remaining European games.

content.headline: Counties interested in signing James Anderson after Lancashire exit
content.shortHeadline: Counties ready to speak to Anderson after Lancashire exit
content.standfirst: Several counties are interested in speaking to James Anderson if he wants to continue playing next summer. The 44-year-old must decide whether to retire or leave Lancashire, where he took 50 Championship wickets last season.

image.caption: James Anderson first played for Lancashire's first team in 2001.

sources.originalTitle: Counties interested in Anderson after Lancs exit

segments.body: Lancashire will not offer Anderson a new contract, ending his playing association with the county where he made his first-team debut in 2001. Clubs in both divisions of the County Championship are interested, and some have already approached him. Anderson had planned to play for another year.

segments.title: A decision still to come
segments.body: Anderson took 50 wickets in Division Two last summer and was Lancashire's County Championship player of the year. Any move may depend on finances, the role offered and the time required away from his home. Whether he continues as a player or retires is not yet known.

content.headline: Ruti Aga receives six-year ban after fake prescription claim
content.shortHeadline: Ruti Aga handed six-year ban for doping and tampering
content.standfirst: The Ethiopian marathon runner tested positive for a prohibited steroid after winning a half-marathon in China. She received a further four-year ban after investigators found the prescription she submitted came from a non-existent clinic.

image.caption: Ruti Aga won the 2019 Tokyo Marathon.

sources.originalTitle: Aga banned for fake prescription from family member

segments.body: Ruti Aga has been banned for six years after testing positive for methylprednisolone and then misleading investigators. The Athletics Integrity Unit said the 32-year-old submitted a prescription from a clinic that did not exist, issued by a family member who was not medically registered. The ban runs from her provisional suspension on 10 September.

content.headline: US to host first Women's Club World Cup in 2028, with Arsenal named
content.shortHeadline: US to host inaugural Women's Club World Cup in 2028
content.standfirst: Fifa has confirmed the United States as host of the first Women's Club World Cup, scheduled for January 2028. Arsenal are among seven clubs already named for the 19-team tournament.

image.caption: The United States will host the first Women's Club World Cup in 2028.

sources.originalTitle: US to host first Women's Club World Cup in 2028

segments.body: The inaugural Women's Club World Cup will run from 5 to 30 January 2028 in the United States. Arsenal, Barcelona, Gotham, Club America, Corinthians, Naegohyang and Wuhan Jiangda have been named; the other 12 places are yet to be determined.

segments.title: A scheduling concern
segments.body: The competition is planned as a 19-team event held every four years. The Women's Super League has previously described its mid-season scheduling as potentially "catastrophic", amid broader concerns about the demands of the women's football calendar.
